title: Structured wine tasting
text: A structured approach to tasting assesses a wine in a fixed order so nothing is missed and wines can be compared consistently: first appearance, then aroma (the nose), then flavour and structure (the palate), and finally conclusions about quality, style and maturity. Working methodically separates objective observation (what the wine is) from preference (whether you like it), which is the basis of professional wine assessment.

title: Wine appearance
text: Appearance is judged for clarity, intensity and colour. White wines deepen from pale lemon-green through gold to amber as they age or see oxidation; reds move from purple in youth toward ruby, garnet and finally tawny with age. A watery rim, deep core, or browning at the edge all give clues to grape, climate, oak and age before the wine is even smelled.

title: The nose (aroma)
text: The nose is assessed for condition (clean or faulty), aroma intensity, and the character of the aromas. Aromas are grouped as primary (from the grape and fermentation, such as fruit, floral and herbaceous notes), secondary (from winemaking, such as yeast, bread and dairy from lees or malolactic conversion), and tertiary (from ageing, such as dried fruit, nut, leather and forest floor).

title: The palate
text: On the palate a taster judges sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavour intensity, flavour characteristics and finish. Taste (sweet, sour, bitter, salt) and mouth-feel (tannin grip, warmth from alcohol, texture) combine with retronasal aroma to build the full flavour picture. Structural components are what let a wine age and pair with food.

title: Acidity in wine
text: Acidity gives wine its freshness and makes the mouth water; it is tasted as a tart, zingy sensation along the sides of the tongue. Grapes from cooler climates and those picked earlier retain more acidity. High acidity keeps a wine lively, balances sweetness, and is a key preservative that helps wines age. Low acidity can make a wine taste flabby or soft.

title: Tannin in wine
text: Tannins are compounds extracted from grape skins, seeds and stems, and from oak, found mainly in red wines. They create a drying, grippy, sometimes bitter sensation on the gums and teeth. Riper grapes and gentler extraction give smoother, rounder tannins; unripe grapes or harsh extraction give green, astringent tannins. Tannin softens with age and pairs well with protein and fat.

title: Alcohol in wine
text: Alcohol comes from yeast fermenting grape sugar, so riper, sweeter grapes yield higher potential alcohol. It is sensed as warmth at the back of the throat and adds body and texture. Light wines sit around 11% ABV, medium 11.5 to 13.9%, and high 14% or more; fortified wines reach 15 to 22%. Balance matters: too much alcohol tastes hot, too little can seem thin.

title: Body in wine
text: Body is the overall impression of weight and fullness in the mouth, from light to full. It results from the combined effect of alcohol, sugar, extract and, in some wines, tannin. A light-bodied wine feels delicate like skimmed milk; a full-bodied wine feels rich and mouth-filling. Warmer climates and riper grapes tend to give fuller-bodied wines.

title: Sweetness and dryness
text: Sweetness describes residual sugar left after fermentation, ranging from bone dry through off-dry and medium to lusciously sweet. A wine is dry when nearly all sugar has been fermented to alcohol. High acidity can make a sweet wine taste fresher and less cloying, which is why the greatest sweet wines balance sugar with vibrant acidity.

title: Flavour intensity and finish
text: Flavour intensity describes how pronounced the flavours are, from light to pronounced. The finish is how long the flavours linger after swallowing: a long, evolving finish is a hallmark of quality, while a short finish that disappears quickly suggests a simpler wine. Length is one of the most reliable indicators of a fine wine.

title: Balance, complexity and quality
text: Quality is assessed through balance (no single component sticking out), length (a persistent finish), intensity of flavour, and complexity (a range of interlinked aromas and flavours). A very good or outstanding wine shows several of these at a high level; a poor wine may be unbalanced, dilute or short. Typicity, how well a wine represents its grape and place, also informs quality.

title: Primary, secondary and tertiary aromas
text: Primary aromas come from the grape and fermentation: fruit, flowers, herbs and spice. Secondary aromas come from post-fermentation winemaking, such as buttery notes from malolactic conversion, or bready, yeasty notes from time on the lees. Tertiary aromas develop with age from oxidation and bottle maturation, giving dried fruit, fig, nut, honey, leather, mushroom and savoury complexity.

title: Aromatic and non-aromatic grapes
text: Aromatic grape varieties such as Muscat, Gewurztraminer, Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc have pronounced, easily recognised aromas even in youth. Non-aromatic or neutral varieties such as Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio and Semillon have subtler grape character and take much of their flavour from where they are grown and how they are made, including oak and lees.

title: Chardonnay
text: Chardonnay is a versatile white grape that reflects climate and winemaking more than strong grape character of its own. Cool climates (Chablis) give lean, high-acid wines with green apple and citrus; warmer climates give riper stone and tropical fruit. Oak adds vanilla, toast and spice, while malolactic conversion and lees ageing add buttery, creamy texture. It is the white grape of white Burgundy and Champagne.

title: Sauvignon Blanc
text: Sauvignon Blanc is an aromatic white grape making crisp, high-acid, unoaked wines with pronounced aromas of gooseberry, elderflower, grass, green pepper and citrus. Cool climates like the Loire (Sancerre) give flinty, restrained styles; Marlborough in New Zealand is famed for pungent, tropical, herbaceous examples. It is usually made for early drinking and is a classic partner for goat cheese.

title: Riesling
text: Riesling is a high-acid, aromatic white grape that ranges from bone dry to intensely sweet and is prized for transparency to place. Youthful aromas include lime, green apple, peach and blossom; with age it develops honeyed, toasty and distinctive petrol-like notes. Its natural acidity balances sweetness beautifully. Germany, Alsace and Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys are benchmark regions.

title: Pinot Gris / Pinot Grigio
text: Pinot Gris and Pinot Grigio are the same grape in different styles. In northern Italy, Pinot Grigio is typically light, dry, crisp and neutral for easy drinking. In Alsace, Pinot Gris is fuller-bodied, richer and often off-dry, with stone fruit, honey and smoky notes. The grape has a pinkish skin and can give wines with more colour and texture than most whites.

title: Chenin Blanc
text: Chenin Blanc is a high-acid white grape of great versatility, making dry, off-dry, sweet, and sparkling wines. Its hallmark aromas are apple, quince, honey and wet wool. The Loire (Vouvray, Savennieres) is its classic French home, producing everything from crisp dry whites to botrytised dessert wines, while South Africa grows large plantings for both everyday and ambitious wines.

title: Semillon
text: Semillon is a white grape with relatively low acidity and waxy, lanolin, citrus and apple character. It is prone to noble rot, making it central to the sweet wines of Sauternes, usually blended with Sauvignon Blanc. In Australia's Hunter Valley it makes distinctive dry whites that age into toasty, honeyed complexity. Oak and blending are common with this grape.

title: Viognier
text: Viognier is a full-bodied, low-acid aromatic white grape giving perfumed wines of apricot, peach, honeysuckle and blossom. Its spiritual home is Condrieu in the northern Rhone. It is often best drunk young while its aromatics are vibrant, and a small amount is sometimes co-fermented with Syrah in Cote-Rotie to stabilise colour and add fragrance.

title: Gewurztraminer
text: Gewurztraminer is an intensely aromatic white grape with low acidity and often high alcohol, giving full-bodied wines of lychee, rose, ginger and exotic spice. Its pink-skinned berries can give a deep golden colour. Alsace is the benchmark region, making dry to sweet styles. Its perfumed character makes it a classic match for aromatic Asian dishes.

title: Gruner Veltliner
text: Gruner Veltliner is Austria's signature white grape, making dry, high-acid, medium-bodied wines with citrus, green fruit, white pepper and a characteristic peppery, herbaceous spice. Styles range from light and zesty to concentrated and age-worthy from top sites in the Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal. It is food-friendly and increasingly popular internationally.

title: Albarino
text: Albarino is an aromatic, high-acid white grape grown in Rias Baixas in north-west Spain and, as Alvarinho, in Portugal's Vinho Verde. It makes fresh, medium-bodied wines with citrus, stone fruit, and often a saline, sometimes slightly floral character. Its zesty acidity and coastal origin make it a natural partner for seafood and shellfish.

title: Muscat
text: Muscat is a family of aromatic grapes with an unmistakable grapey, floral, orange-blossom perfume, one of the few grapes whose wine actually smells of grapes. It makes styles from dry (Alsace) to lightly sparkling and sweet (Moscato d'Asti) to rich fortified wines. Muscat of Alexandria and Muscat Blanc a Petits Grains are the most important members.

title: Cabernet Sauvignon
text: Cabernet Sauvignon is a black grape making full-bodied, deeply coloured, high-tannin, high-acid reds built to age. Classic aromas are blackcurrant, black cherry, cedar, mint and, when less ripe, green bell pepper. It is the backbone of the Medoc in Bordeaux, usually blended with Merlot, and thrives in Napa Valley, Coonawarra, Maipo and beyond. Oak ageing adds cedar and spice.

title: Merlot
text: Merlot is a black grape giving medium to full-bodied reds with softer tannins and higher alcohol than Cabernet Sauvignon, showing plum, black cherry, chocolate and herbal notes. It ripens earlier and makes approachable wines. It dominates the Right Bank of Bordeaux (Saint-Emilion, Pomerol) and is widely planted worldwide, often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon to add flesh and roundness.

title: Pinot Noir
text: Pinot Noir is a thin-skinned black grape making light to medium-bodied reds with pale colour, high acidity, low to medium tannin, and delicate red-fruit aromas of strawberry, cherry and raspberry, developing forest floor and game with age. It is difficult to grow and site-sensitive. Burgundy is its benchmark, with fine examples from Oregon, Central Otago, Sonoma and Germany (as Spatburgunder).

title: Syrah / Shiraz
text: Syrah, called Shiraz in Australia, is a black grape making deeply coloured, full-bodied reds with medium to high tannin and flavours of blackberry, black pepper, and, in warm climates, ripe plum and liquorice. Cool-climate northern Rhone (Hornitage, Cote-Rotie) gives peppery, savoury styles; warm Barossa gives rich, sweet-fruited, sometimes chocolatey wines. It responds well to oak.

title: Grenache / Garnacha
text: Grenache (Garnacha in Spain) is a black grape giving medium to full-bodied reds that are high in alcohol with soft tannins and red-fruit, strawberry, and spicy, sometimes herbal character. It is a key blending grape in the southern Rhone (Chateauneuf-du-Pape) and in Spanish Priorat and Rioja. It also makes pale, fruity roses and thrives in hot, dry, windy climates.

title: Tempranillo
text: Tempranillo is Spain's leading black grape, making medium to full-bodied reds with medium acidity and tannin and flavours of red cherry, plum, tomato leaf and, with oak and age, leather, tobacco and vanilla. It is the backbone of Rioja and Ribera del Duero. Traditional Rioja spends long periods in American oak, giving its signature dill and coconut-tinged, savoury style.

title: Sangiovese
text: Sangiovese is the leading black grape of central Italy, making high-acid, high-tannin, medium-bodied reds with sour red cherry, plum, dried herb and savoury, earthy notes. It is the grape of Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. Its bright acidity and grippy tannins make it a natural match for tomato-based Italian food.

title: Nebbiolo
text: Nebbiolo is the noble black grape of Piedmont, making pale but powerful reds with very high tannin and acidity that belie their light colour, and aromas of tar, roses, red cherry, and dried herbs. It is the grape of Barolo and Barbaresco, wines that demand ageing to soften their formidable structure and develop savoury, truffled complexity.

title: Malbec
text: Malbec is a black grape making deeply coloured, full-bodied reds with ripe black fruit, plum and floral violet notes and medium to high, generally smooth tannins. Originally from south-west France (Cahors), it found international fame in Argentina, especially high-altitude Mendoza, where it produces plush, fruit-forward wines that are approachable yet age-worthy.

title: Zinfandel / Primitivo
text: Zinfandel, genetically the same as Italy's Primitivo, is a black grape making bold, high-alcohol reds with jammy brambly fruit, sweet spice and sometimes a raisined edge from uneven ripening. California is its stronghold for rich dry reds; it is also the base of off-dry pink White Zinfandel. Its ripeness and generosity suit barbecue and rich meats.

title: Cabernet Franc
text: Cabernet Franc is a black grape making medium-bodied reds with medium tannin, higher acidity, and aromas of red fruit, leafy herbaceousness, graphite and violet. It ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon and adds fragrance and freshness to Bordeaux blends. In the Loire (Chinon, Bourgueil) it makes distinctive varietal reds, and it is a parent of both Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.

title: Gamay
text: Gamay is a black grape making light-bodied, low-tannin, high-acid reds with bright red-cherry and raspberry fruit, often with a bubblegum or banana note when made by carbonic maceration. It is the grape of Beaujolais in southern Burgundy. The best cru Beaujolais villages produce more structured, age-worthy reds, while Beaujolais Nouveau is released young and fruity weeks after harvest.

title: Mourvedre
text: Mourvedre (Monastrell in Spain, Mataro elsewhere) is a black grape needing heat to ripen, giving full-bodied, deeply coloured reds with high tannin and gamey, meaty, blackberry and herbal notes. It is a key partner to Grenache and Syrah in southern Rhone GSM blends and in Bandol, where it dominates age-worthy, structured reds. It can show a slightly wild, animal character.

title: Bordeaux red wines
text: Red Bordeaux is a blend, chiefly of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot with Cabernet Franc and sometimes Petit Verdot. The gravelly Left Bank (Medoc, Graves) favours structured, tannic, blackcurrant-and-cedar Cabernet-led wines; the clay Right Bank (Saint-Emilion, Pomerol) favours plush, plummy Merlot-led wines. The blend hedges against vintage variation in this moderate maritime climate.

title: Bordeaux Left Bank and 1855 classification
text: The Left Bank of Bordeaux includes the Medoc communes of Saint-Estephe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux, plus Graves. Its top estates were ranked into five growths (crus) in the 1855 Classification, based on the prices their wines fetched. Cabernet Sauvignon leads these blends, giving firm tannin, blackcurrant and cedar, and the capacity to age for decades.

title: Bordeaux Right Bank
text: The Right Bank of Bordeaux, centred on Saint-Emilion and Pomerol, sits on cooler clay and limestone soils that suit Merlot and Cabernet Franc. The wines are typically softer, rounder and more approachable young than Left Bank wines, with plum, fruitcake and chocolate character. Pomerol has no formal classification but includes some of the world's most sought-after estates.

title: Sauternes and botrytis sweet wine
text: Sauternes, in southern Bordeaux, makes luscious sweet wines from Semillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle affected by noble rot (Botrytis cinerea). The fungus dehydrates ripe grapes, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour and adding honeyed, dried-apricot, marmalade complexity. Yields are tiny and picking is done grape by grape, making these wines rare and expensive.

title: Burgundy
text: Burgundy in eastern France makes some of the world's most revered wines almost entirely from two grapes: Chardonnay for whites and Pinot Noir for reds. The region is defined by terroir, with a mosaic of vineyards ranked from regional and village wines up through Premier Cru to Grand Cru. Its cool continental climate gives elegant, high-acid, site-expressive wines.

title: Chablis
text: Chablis, in the cool north of Burgundy, makes bone-dry, high-acid Chardonnay with green apple, citrus, and a distinctive flinty, mineral character often attributed to its Kimmeridgian limestone soils. Most Chablis sees little or no new oak, preserving purity and tension. The best Premier and Grand Cru sites give more concentrated, age-worthy wines.

title: Cote d'Or
text: The Cote d'Or is the heart of Burgundy, split into the Cote de Nuits (mostly great Pinot Noir, in villages such as Gevrey-Chambertin and Vosne-Romanee) and the Cote de Beaune (celebrated white Burgundy from Puligny- and Chassagne-Montrachet plus fine reds). Tiny, individually named vineyards and a strict cru hierarchy define quality and price here.

title: Beaujolais
text: Beaujolais, at the southern end of Burgundy, makes light, juicy, low-tannin reds from the Gamay grape, often via carbonic maceration for bright, fruity flavours. Beaujolais Nouveau is released just weeks after harvest, but the ten named cru villages such as Morgon and Fleurie make more serious, structured wines from granite soils that can age.

title: Champagne
text: Champagne is a cool region in northern France making sparkling wine by the traditional method, chiefly from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier. A second fermentation in the bottle traps carbon dioxide, and extended ageing on the lees gives its hallmark bready, biscuity autolytic character alongside high acidity. Most is non-vintage blended for a consistent house style.

title: Loire Valley
text: The Loire is a long, cool French river region famous for crisp whites. Sancerre and Pouilly-Fume make flinty Sauvignon Blanc; Vouvray and Savennieres make Chenin Blanc from dry to sweet; Muscadet near the Atlantic makes lean, saline whites often aged on lees. Chinon and Bourgueil make herbaceous Cabernet Franc reds. High acidity is the thread linking the region.

title: Northern Rhone
text: The Northern Rhone is a cool-influenced region where Syrah is the only black grape, making peppery, savoury, structured reds in appellations such as Hermitage, Cote-Rotie and Cornas. A little Viognier may be co-fermented with Syrah in Cote-Rotie. White grapes Viognier (Condrieu), Marsanne and Roussanne make full-bodied whites. Steep granite slopes define the best sites.

title: Southern Rhone
text: The Southern Rhone is warmer and makes mostly blended reds led by Grenache with Syrah and Mourvedre (the GSM blend). Chateauneuf-du-Pape is its most famous appellation, permitting many grape varieties and known for full-bodied, spicy, warming reds. Cotes du Rhone provides great-value everyday reds. The Mistral wind and stony soils shape the wines.

title: Alsace
text: Alsace, in sheltered north-east France, is unusual for France in labelling wines by grape variety. It makes aromatic, mostly dry to off-dry whites from Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat, plus sweet late-harvest styles. Protected by the Vosges mountains, it is sunny and dry, giving ripe, expressive, full-flavoured wines with pronounced aromatics.

title: Tuscany and Chianti
text: Tuscany in central Italy is the home of Sangiovese, the grape behind Chianti and Chianti Classico. These are high-acid, medium-bodied reds with sour cherry, herb and savoury notes, well suited to food. Super Tuscans, using international grapes like Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot or unblended Sangiovese, emerged outside traditional rules and gained international acclaim.

title: Brunello di Montalcino
text: Brunello di Montalcino is a prestigious Tuscan red made entirely from a local Sangiovese clone around the town of Montalcino. Warmer and drier than the Chianti heartland, it gives powerful, concentrated, tannic wines requiring years of ageing, including mandatory time in oak, before release. The wines are savoury, structured and long-lived.

title: Piedmont: Barolo and Barbaresco
text: Piedmont in north-west Italy makes Barolo and Barbaresco from the Nebbiolo grape: pale, powerful reds with very high tannin and acidity, tar-and-roses aromatics, and great ageing potential. Barbaresco is generally a touch softer and earlier-maturing than Barolo. The region also makes juicy Barbera and light, aromatic Dolcetto reds, plus sweet sparkling Moscato d'Asti.

title: Veneto: Soave, Valpolicella and Amarone
text: The Veneto in north-east Italy makes crisp white Soave from the Garganega grape, and light, cherry-scented Valpolicella reds from Corvina. Amarone della Valpolicella is a rich, full-bodied dry red made from grapes dried for months to concentrate sugar and flavour (the appassimento method), giving high alcohol and raisined, savoury intensity.

title: Prosecco
text: Prosecco is Italy's popular sparkling wine, made in the Veneto and Friuli from the Glera grape. Unlike Champagne, its second fermentation takes place in a pressurised tank (the tank or Charmat method), which preserves fresh, fruity, floral, pear-and-apple aromas rather than developing bready autolytic character. It is typically light, off-dry and made for early drinking.

title: Rioja
text: Rioja in northern Spain makes its most famous wines from Tempranillo, often with Garnacha. Traditional styles age long in American oak, giving savoury, vanilla, coconut and dill notes over red fruit and leather. Wines are labelled by ageing: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva indicate increasing time in oak and bottle before release. Rioja also makes fresh and barrel-aged whites.

title: Ribera del Duero
text: Ribera del Duero, on Spain's high central plateau, makes powerful reds from Tempranillo (locally called Tinto Fino or Tinta del Pais). Its extreme continental climate, with hot days and cold nights at altitude, gives deeply coloured, concentrated, structured wines with firm tannins and dark fruit, generally richer and more intense than typical Rioja.

title: Rias Baixas
text: Rias Baixas in cool, wet, green north-west Spain (Galicia) specialises in the Albarino grape, making fresh, aromatic, high-acid whites with citrus, stone fruit and a saline coastal character. The maritime climate and proximity to the Atlantic make these wines a natural partner for the region's abundant seafood. Most are unoaked and made for early drinking.

title: Cava
text: Cava is Spain's traditional-method sparkling wine, made mostly in Catalonia from local grapes Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada, sometimes with Chardonnay or Pinot Noir. Like Champagne it undergoes a second fermentation and lees ageing in bottle, giving fresh citrus and apple fruit with a subtle bready character, usually at a very approachable price.

title: Sherry
text: Sherry is a fortified wine from Jerez in southern Spain, made chiefly from Palomino. Styles range from bone-dry Fino and Manzanilla, aged under a protective film of flor yeast that gives a tangy, savoury character, to oxidatively aged Amontillado and rich, nutty Oloroso. Sweet styles use Pedro Ximenez. Sherry is matured in a fractional blending system called the solera.

title: German wine and the Pradikat system
text: Germany's cool climate produces some of the world's finest Riesling, from bone dry to lusciously sweet, marked by piercing acidity and low to moderate alcohol. Quality wines are graded by ripeness at harvest (the Pradikat scale): Kabinett, Spatlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, with Eiswein from frozen grapes. Dry wines are often labelled trocken.

title: Mosel
text: The Mosel is a cool German region where Riesling grows on steep, slate slopes above the river. The wines are typically light in body and alcohol, with racy acidity, delicate green apple, citrus and peach fruit, and often a touch of sweetness balanced by that acidity. Slate soils are associated with a flinty, mineral character in the best sites.

title: Douro and Port
text: The Douro Valley in northern Portugal makes Port, a sweet fortified red wine, by adding grape spirit during fermentation to stop it early, retaining natural grape sweetness. Styles include fruity Ruby and Late Bottled Vintage, nutty oxidative Tawny aged in cask, and the finest Vintage Port aged in bottle. Native grapes like Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca dominate. Unfortified Douro reds are also excellent.

title: Vinho Verde
text: Vinho Verde from north-west Portugal is typically a light, low-alcohol, high-acid white, often with a slight spritz, made for early drinking. The name means green (young) wine, referring to its youthful freshness rather than colour. Better examples are made from the Alvarinho (Albarino) grape and show more concentration and citrus, stone-fruit character.

title: Madeira
text: Madeira is a fortified wine from the Portuguese island of the same name, uniquely made by deliberately heating the wine (estufagem or canteiro), which gives it remarkable resistance to oxidation and a long life. Styles run from dry to sweet, named after grapes Sercial, Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey, all sharing high acidity and cooked, caramelised, nutty flavours.

title: Napa Valley
text: Napa Valley in California is the United States' most prestigious wine region, best known for rich, full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon with ripe blackcurrant, cassis and oak-derived spice. Its warm days, cooler nights and diverse soils and sub-regions (such as Oakville and Rutherford) give powerful, age-worthy reds. It also produces highly regarded Chardonnay.

title: Sonoma
text: Sonoma County, on the California coast north of San Francisco, is more diverse and cooler in parts than neighbouring Napa. Fog-influenced areas like the Russian River Valley and Sonoma Coast excel with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, while warmer inland zones make Zinfandel and Cabernet Sauvignon. The maritime influence lends freshness to its wines.

title: Oregon
text: Oregon, in the cool Pacific North-West of the USA, is celebrated for Pinot Noir, especially from the Willamette Valley. Its cool, marginal climate gives elegant, high-acid, red-fruited wines often compared to Burgundy in style. Pinot Gris and Chardonnay are the leading whites. Vintage variation matters here because ripening is never guaranteed.

title: Marlborough, New Zealand
text: Marlborough, at the top of New Zealand's South Island, made its name with pungent, intensely aromatic Sauvignon Blanc showing gooseberry, passionfruit, tropical fruit and fresh-cut grass, with vibrant acidity. The cool, sunny, maritime climate and long ripening season concentrate aromatics. The region also makes fine Pinot Noir and aromatic whites.

title: Central Otago
text: Central Otago, in the south of New Zealand's South Island, is one of the world's most southerly wine regions and its only significantly continental one. Its warm days and cold nights at altitude give ripe yet fresh Pinot Noir with concentrated dark cherry fruit, floral notes and firm structure. It is New Zealand's benchmark region for the grape.

title: Barossa Valley
text: The Barossa Valley in South Australia is famous for rich, full-bodied Shiraz with ripe blackberry, plum, sweet spice and chocolate, often from very old, low-yielding vines. Its warm climate gives generous, high-alcohol, powerful reds. Grenache and Mourvedre also feature, sometimes blended with Shiraz. The cooler Eden Valley subregion excels with Riesling.

title: Margaret River
text: Margaret River in Western Australia is a maritime region prized for structured Cabernet Sauvignon (sometimes blended with Merlot) and for high-quality Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc-Semillon blends. Its moderate, ocean-tempered climate gives balanced, elegant wines. It is regarded as one of Australia's premium quality regions despite its relatively small output.

title: Hunter Valley Semillon
text: The Hunter Valley, north of Sydney in Australia, is renowned for a distinctive dry Semillon: picked early, it is low in alcohol and high in acidity, austere and lemony when young, but ages in bottle into a rich, honeyed, toasty wine without any oak. It is one of the wine world's most singular and long-lived white styles.

title: Stellenbosch and South Africa
text: Stellenbosch is South Africa's leading quality wine region, near Cape Town, making structured Cabernet Sauvignon, Bordeaux blends, Shiraz and Chardonnay in a warm, mountain-influenced climate. South Africa is also known for Chenin Blanc, its most planted grape, and Pinotage, a local crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsault that gives bold, sometimes smoky reds.

title: Mendoza and Argentine Malbec
text: Mendoza, in the rain-shadow of the Andes, is Argentina's dominant wine region and the world capital of Malbec. High-altitude vineyards enjoy intense sunlight and cool nights, giving deeply coloured, full-bodied reds with ripe plum and blackberry fruit, floral notes and smooth tannins. Irrigation from Andean meltwater makes viticulture possible in this dry, high desert.

title: Chile
text: Chile is a long, narrow country protected by the Andes and Pacific, making reliable, good-value wines across many styles. Its Central Valley grows Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and its signature grape Carmenere, which gives herbaceous, spicy, plummy reds. Cooler coastal areas like Casablanca make crisp Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay. The dry climate suits organic viticulture.

title: Carmenere
text: Carmenere is a black grape once widespread in Bordeaux and now Chile's signature variety, where it was long confused with Merlot. It makes medium to full-bodied reds with ripe red and black fruit, marked herbaceous, green-pepper and spicy notes, and soft tannins. It needs a long, warm season to ripen fully and avoid overly green, pyrazine-dominated flavours.

title: Fermentation
text: Alcoholic fermentation is the process by which yeast converts grape sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide, turning grape juice into wine. Winemakers choose ambient wild yeasts or cultured strains, and control temperature: cooler fermentations preserve delicate fruit and floral aromas in whites, while warmer fermentations extract more colour and tannin in reds. Stopping fermentation early leaves residual sweetness.

title: Malolactic conversion
text: Malolactic conversion (or fermentation) is a bacterial process that turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, lowering perceived acidity and adding a rounder texture and buttery, creamy notes. It is standard for nearly all red wines and used selectively for whites such as many Chardonnays. It is often avoided in crisp, aromatic whites to keep their fresh, zesty acidity.

title: Oak influence
text: Oak vessels shape wine through flavour and slow oxygen exchange. New oak barrels add vanilla, toast, smoke, clove and coconut (American oak) or subtler spice (French oak); older or larger vessels add texture and gentle oxidation with little flavour. Toasting level and barrel size affect intensity. Oak also softens tannins and stabilises colour in reds over time.

title: Lees ageing and sur lie
text: Lees are the dead yeast cells left after fermentation. Ageing a wine on its lees (sur lie), sometimes with stirring (batonnage), adds body, a creamy texture, and savoury, bready, biscuity flavours. It is central to the character of Champagne and other traditional-method sparkling wines, and to styles like Muscadet sur lie and many barrel-fermented Chardonnays.

title: Maceration and skin contact
text: Maceration is the soaking of grape juice on skins to extract colour, tannin and flavour compounds; it is essential to red winemaking and to orange (skin-contact) white wines. Longer, warmer maceration extracts more; gentler, shorter maceration gives lighter, fresher wines. Techniques like punching down and pumping over keep the floating cap of skins in contact with the juice.

title: Carbonic maceration
text: Carbonic maceration ferments whole, uncrushed grapes in a carbon-dioxide-rich environment, so fermentation begins inside each intact berry. It produces bright colour, very low tannin, and distinctive fruity, sometimes bubblegum or banana aromas. It is strongly associated with Beaujolais and Gamay, and is used to make soft, juicy, early-drinking reds elsewhere too.

title: Traditional method sparkling wine
text: The traditional method creates bubbles through a second fermentation inside the sealed bottle, trapping carbon dioxide. After ageing on the lees, sediment is worked into the neck (riddling), frozen and expelled (disgorgement), and a dosage of wine and sugar sets the final sweetness. This labour-intensive method gives fine, persistent bubbles and bready complexity, as in Champagne, Cava and English sparkling wine.

title: Tank method sparkling wine
text: In the tank method (also called Charmat), the second fermentation happens in a large pressurised tank rather than individual bottles, and the wine is then filtered and bottled under pressure. It is faster and cheaper and preserves fresh, primary fruit and floral aromas, making it ideal for aromatic sparklers like Prosecco and Asti rather than developing autolytic, bready character.

title: Fortification
text: Fortified wines have grape spirit added to raise alcohol to roughly 15 to 22 percent. Adding spirit during fermentation stops the yeast and leaves natural sweetness, as in Port; adding it after a dry fermentation gives dry styles like Fino Sherry. The higher alcohol acts as a preservative, historically allowing wines to survive long sea voyages. Examples include Port, Sherry, Madeira and Marsala.

title: Noble rot sweet wines
text: Noble rot is the beneficial form of the fungus Botrytis cinerea, which in the right damp-then-dry conditions punctures ripe grape skins and dehydrates the berries. This concentrates sugar, acid and flavour and adds honey, dried apricot and marmalade complexity. It produces the great sweet wines of Sauternes, Tokaji and German Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.

title: Late harvest and ice wine
text: Sweet wines can be made by leaving grapes on the vine to over-ripen and shrivel (late harvest), concentrating their sugars. Ice wine (Eiswein) goes further: grapes are left until they freeze on the vine and are pressed while frozen, so water stays behind as ice and only concentrated sweet juice is extracted. Both rely on high acidity to stay balanced and fresh.

title: Dried-grape (passito) wines
text: In the appassimento or passito method, harvested grapes are dried on mats or racks for weeks or months, losing water and concentrating sugar and flavour before fermentation. This can make rich dry wines like Amarone della Valpolicella or sweet wines like Vin Santo and Recioto. The technique gives high alcohol, intensity, and often raisined, figgy character.

title: Rose production
text: Most rose is made by giving red grapes brief skin contact (a few hours) so the juice takes on colour but little tannin, then fermenting like a white wine; longer contact gives deeper colour. Alternatively, saignee bleeds off pink juice from a red fermentation. Provence is famed for pale, dry, delicate roses. Blending red and white wine is generally only permitted for rose Champagne.

title: Blending
text: Blending combines different grape varieties, vineyard parcels, or vintages to build balance, complexity and consistency. Classic blends include Bordeaux (Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot), southern Rhone GSM (Grenache, Syrah, Mourvedre), and Champagne (Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier). Blending lets winemakers offset a weak vintage, add structure, or achieve a repeatable house style year after year.

title: Climate and wine style
text: Climate strongly shapes wine style. Cool climates give grapes with higher acidity, lower sugar (so lower alcohol), and lighter, more herbaceous or tart-fruit flavours. Warm climates give riper grapes with lower acidity, higher sugar and alcohol, and richer, jammier fruit. The distinction between cool, moderate and warm climate helps predict a wine's body, acidity and flavour profile.

title: Old World and New World
text: Old World refers to traditional European wine regions such as France, Italy and Spain, where wines are usually labelled by place and made in restrained, often higher-acid, earthy styles governed by strict rules. New World refers to regions like the USA, Australia, Chile and South Africa, where wines are often labelled by grape variety and tend toward riper, fruit-forward, fuller styles, though these generalisations blur increasingly.

title: Vintage variation
text: Vintage is the year the grapes were harvested, and it matters because weather changes each year. In marginal, cool climates like Bordeaux or Burgundy, a warm sunny year can produce ripe, age-worthy wines while a cold, wet year gives leaner, lighter ones. In reliably warm climates, vintage variation is smaller. Non-vintage wines blend years to smooth out these differences.

title: Soil and terroir
text: Terroir is the combination of soil, climate, topography and local tradition that gives a wine its sense of place. Soils influence drainage, heat retention and vine vigour: gravel warms and drains well (Medoc), limestone and clay retain water (Burgundy, Chablis), and slate stores heat (Mosel). While the direct flavour contribution of soil is debated, its effect on vine growth clearly shapes wine style.

title: Vineyard hazards
text: Grapes face many growing-season hazards: spring frost can kill young shoots, hail can destroy a crop, and rain at flowering or harvest causes poor fruit set or dilution and rot. Excessive heat can scorch grapes or stall ripening, while drought stresses vines. Fungal diseases like powdery and downy mildew thrive in damp conditions, and pests such as phylloxera devastated vineyards historically.

title: Organic and biodynamic viticulture
text: Organic viticulture avoids synthetic pesticides, herbicides and fertilisers, relying on natural methods to manage the vineyard. Biodynamic viticulture goes further, treating the farm as a single organism and following a lunar and cosmic calendar with specific herbal and mineral preparations. Both aim to improve vine health and expression of terroir; sustainable schemes offer a broader, less strict middle path.

title: Serving temperature
text: Serving temperature affects how a wine shows. Sparkling and light, crisp whites are best well chilled (around 6 to 10 C) to keep them refreshing; fuller whites and light reds suit around 10 to 13 C; medium and full-bodied reds show best lightly cool at 15 to 18 C, below typical room temperature. Too warm makes alcohol dominate; too cold mutes aromas and exaggerates tannin and acidity.

title: Decanting
text: Decanting pours wine off into another vessel for two reasons: to separate an older wine from its sediment, and to aerate a young, tightly wound wine so it opens up and softens. Robust young reds often benefit from aeration; fragile old wines are decanted gently just before serving to avoid losing their delicate aromas. Not all wines need decanting.

title: Glassware
text: Glass shape influences perception. A larger bowl lets aromas gather and concentrate, benefiting complex reds; a narrower flute or tulip preserves the bubbles and aromatics of sparkling wine. Clear, thin, stemmed glasses filled only about a third full let you see, swirl and smell the wine properly. The stem keeps the hand from warming the wine.

title: Storing and ageing wine
text: Wine is best stored on its side (for corked bottles) in a cool, dark, humid place at a stable temperature around 10 to 15 C, away from light, heat and vibration. Most wine is made to drink young; only a minority improve with age, softening tannins and developing tertiary complexity. High acidity, tannin, sugar or alcohol all help a wine age well.

title: Food and wine pairing basics
text: The goal of pairing is balance so neither the food nor the wine overwhelms the other. Matching intensity is key: delicate dishes suit light wines, rich dishes suit fuller ones. Pairings can complement (buttery lobster with rich Chardonnay) or contrast (sweet wine with salty blue cheese). Consider the dish's dominant elements, not just the main protein.

title: How food affects wine: acidity, salt and sweetness
text: Certain food elements change how wine tastes. High-acid and salty foods make wine seem softer, richer and fruitier, so acidic wines pair well with acidic or salty dishes. Sweetness in food makes wine taste less sweet and more acidic and tannic, so a dessert wine should be at least as sweet as the dish. Umami can make wines seem harsher, which acidity helps offset.

title: How food affects wine: tannin and fat
text: Tannic red wines pair classically with protein- and fat-rich foods such as steak: the protein and fat soften the drying grip of the tannins, making the wine feel smoother while cutting through the richness of the dish. Conversely, tannic wines can taste harsh and metallic with spicy, salty, or delicate fish dishes, which is why bold reds and sushi rarely match well.

title: Cork taint (TCA)
text: Cork taint is a common wine fault caused chiefly by the compound TCA, which can form in natural cork and taints the wine. It mutes fruit and gives musty, damp-cardboard, wet-dog smells. It is harmless but unpleasant and renders the wine unappealing. Its prevalence is one reason many producers now use screwcaps or technical closures, especially for whites meant to be drunk young.

title: Oxidation and reduction
text: Oxidation occurs when a wine gets too much oxygen, dulling fresh fruit and giving flat, sherry-like, bruised-apple or nutty notes and browning colour; it is a fault in wines meant to be fresh but deliberate in styles like Oloroso Sherry. Reduction is the opposite, from a lack of oxygen, giving struggle-to-shift smells of struck match, rubber, or rotten egg, which can sometimes blow off with aeration.

title: Brettanomyces and volatile acidity
text: Brettanomyces (brett) is a spoilage yeast that produces animal, farmyard, sticking-plaster or smoky aromas; small amounts divide opinion as adding complexity, but high levels are a fault. Volatile acidity (VA) at excessive levels gives vinegary or nail-varnish (acetone) smells. Both are winemaking faults linked to hygiene and oxygen exposure, though tiny amounts are present in many wines.

title: EU quality labels: PDO and PGI
text: European Union wine law uses two main quality categories tied to origin. Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) covers wines from a defined area made under strict rules on grapes, yields and methods, and includes traditional terms like France's AOC and Italy's DOC and DOCG. Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) is a broader, more flexible category, covering wines like French IGP and Italian IGT.

title: French appellation system (AOC)
text: France's Appellation d'Origine Controlee (AOC or AOP) guarantees a wine comes from a named place and follows rules on permitted grapes, maximum yields, and winemaking. It says nothing directly about quality but signals typicity. Regions are often nested, from broad (Bordeaux AOC) to specific (a single village or vineyard), with narrower appellations generally implying higher potential quality.

title: Italian classification: DOC and DOCG
text: Italy's quality pyramid runs from generic Vino up through IGT (broad regional wines), DOC (defined origin with rules), and DOCG at the top, where wines face stricter rules and official tasting before release. The G stands for Guarantita. Well-known DOCG wines include Barolo, Barbaresco, Chianti Classico and Brunello di Montalcino. The system is based on origin, not a guarantee of taste.

title: Spanish classification and ageing terms
text: Spain's system includes DO (Denominacion de Origen) and the higher DOCa or DOQ, held by only Rioja and Priorat. Spain also labels many reds by ageing: Joven is young and unoaked; Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva indicate progressively longer minimum ageing in oak and bottle before release, with Gran Reserva reserved for the best vintages and longest maturation.

title: New World labelling and varietal wines
text: New World wines are commonly labelled by grape variety, such as Chardonnay or Shiraz, making them easy for consumers to choose. Rules on how much of the named grape must be present vary by country. Regions of origin are also indicated, and single-vineyard bottlings signal a more specific, often higher-quality expression. This varietal labelling contrasts with the Old World focus on place.
